0|How long do I have to notify the autho.q: How long do I have to notify the authority about a data breach?
0|How long do I have to notify the autho.answer:
The controller must notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, if feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach, unless the breach is unlikely to risk individuals’ rights and freedoms. [Art. 33(1), p. 52]

Sources:
- Art. 33(1), p. 52: "In the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55, unless the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons."

0|What is the right to be forgotten?.q: What is the right to be forgotten?
0|What is the right to be forgotten?.answer:
- The right to be forgotten lets a data subject request the controller erase their personal data without undue delay. [Art. 17(1), p. 43-44]
- The text states: "Paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to the extent that processing is necessary" [Art. 17(3), p. 44]

Sources:
- Art. 17(1), p. 43-44: "The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller the erasure of personal data concerning him or her without undue delay and the controller shall have the obligation to erase personal data without undue delay where one of the following grounds applies:"
- Art. 17(3), p. 44: "Paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to the extent that processing is necessary:"

0|What is the maximum fine for the most.q: What is the maximum fine for the most serious infringements?
0|What is the maximum fine for the most.answer:
The most serious infringements can be fined up to €20 million or 4 % of worldwide turnover, whichever is higher. [Art. 83(5), p. 83][Art. 83(6), p. 83]

Sources:
- Art. 83(5), p. 83: "Infringements of the following provisions shall, in accordance with paragraph 2, be subject to administrative fines up to 20 000 000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher:"
- Art. 83(6), p. 83: "Non-compliance with an order by the supervisory authority as referred to in Article 58(2) shall, in accordance with paragraph 2 of this Article, be subject to administrative fines up to 20 000 000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher."

0|What are the principles for processing.q: What are the principles for processing personal data?
0|What are the principles for processing.answer:
- Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently with respect to the data subject. [Art. 5(1), p. 35-36]
- Data may only be collected for specific, explicit, legitimate purposes and not further processed incompatibly. [Art. 5(1), p. 35-36]
- Processing must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for its purpose. [Art. 5(1), p. 35-36]
- Personal data must be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date. [Art. 5(1), p. 35-36]
- Data should be retained only as long as necessary for the purposes for which it is processed. [Art. 5(1), p. 35-36]
- Processing must ensure appropriate security to protect data against unauthorized or unlawful handling and accidental loss. [Art. 5(1), p. 35-36]

Sources:
- Art. 5(1), p. 35-36: "(a) processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject (‘lawfulness, fairness and transparency’); | (b) collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes; | (c) adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (‘data minimisation’); | (d) accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date; | (e) kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed; | (f) processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures (‘integrity and confidentiality’)."

0|Can a data subject withdraw consent at.q: Can a data subject withdraw consent at any time?
0|Can a data subject withdraw consent at.answer:
A data subject can withdraw consent at any time, and this does not affect the lawfulness of processing that occurred before the withdrawal. [Art. 7, p. 37]

Sources:
- Art. 7, p. 37: "The data subject shall have the right to withdraw his or her consent at any time. The withdrawal of consent shall not affect the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal."

0|What is the age limit for a child's co.q: What is the age limit for a child's consent to online services?
0|What is the age limit for a child's co.answer:
Processing of a child's personal data for online services is lawful only if the child is at least 16, or if a lower age set by law (but not below 13) permits consent by a parent or guardian. [Art. 8, p. 37-38]

Sources:
- Art. 8, p. 37-38: "Where the child is below the age of 16 years, such processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility over the child. Member States may provide by law for a lower age for those purposes provided that such lower age is not below 13 years."

0|What is the right of access by the dat.q: What is the right of access by the data subject?
0|What is the right of access by the dat.answer:
- The data subject can ask the controller to confirm if personal data are being processed and, if so, receive access to those data. [Art. 15(1), p. 43]
- The access right includes information on the processing purposes, data categories, recipients (including third‑country or international organisations), storage period, related rights, complaints, source and automated decision‑making. [Art. 15(1), p. 43]
- If personal data are transferred abroad, the data subject must be informed of the safeguards applied under Article 46. [Art. 15(2), p. 43]
- The controller must give the data subject a copy of the personal data being processed. [Art. 15(3), p. 43]
- For additional copies, the controller may charge a reasonable fee covering administrative costs. [Art. 15(3), p. 43]
- When the request is made electronically, the information must be supplied in a commonly used electronic format unless the data subject asks otherwise. [Art. 15(3), p. 43]
- Obtaining a copy must not adversely affect the rights and freedoms of other persons. [Art. 15(4), p. 43]

Sources:
- Art. 15(1), p. 43: "The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller confirmation as to whether or not personal data concerning him or her are being processed, and, where that is the case, access to the personal data and the following information: | (a) the purposes of the processing; (b) the categories of personal data concerned; (c) the recipients or categories of recipient to whom the personal data have been or will be disclosed, in particular recipients in third countries or international organisations;"
- Art. 15(2), p. 43: "Where personal data are transferred to a third country or to an international organisation, the data subject shall have the right to be informed of the appropriate safeguards pursuant to Article 46 relating to the transfer."
- Art. 15(3), p. 43: "The controller shall provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing. | For any further copies requested by the data subject, the controller may charge a reasonable fee based on administrative costs. | Where the data subject makes the request by electronic means, and unless otherwise requested by the data subject, the information shall be provided in a commonly used electronic form."
- Art. 15(4), p. 43: "The right to obtain a copy referred to in paragraph 3 shall not adversely affect the rights and freedoms of others."

0|What is the right to data portability?.q: What is the right to data portability?
0|What is the right to data portability?.answer:
- The data subject has the right to receive personal data they provided in a structured, commonly used, machine‑readable format. [Art. 20, p. 45]
- The right applies only when the processing is based on consent or a contract. [Art. 20, p. 45]
- The right also requires that the processing be carried out by automated means. [Art. 20, p. 45]
- Where technically feasible, the data subject may have the personal data transmitted directly from one controller to another. [Art. 20, p. 45]
- The right does not apply to processing necessary for a public‑interest task or the exercise of official authority. [Art. 20, p. 45]

(Note: 1 statement(s) could not be verified against the text and were removed.)

Sources:
- Art. 20, p. 45: "The data subject shall have the right to receive the personal data concerning him or her, which he or she has provided to a controller, in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format and have the right to transmit those data to another controller without hindrance from the controller to which the personal data have been provided, where: | 1. (a) the processing is based on consent pursuant to point (a) of Article 6(1) or point (a) of Article 9(2) or on a contract pursuant to point (b) of Article 6(1); 2. | and (b) the processing is carried out by automated means. | The data subject shall have the right to receive the personal data concerning him or her, which he or she has provided to a controller, in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format and have the right to transmit those data to another controller without hindrance from the controller to which the personal data have been provided, where: In exercising his or her right to data portability pursuant to paragraph 1, the data subject shall have the right to have the personal data… | That right shall not apply to processing necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller."

0|What is the right to rectification?.q: What is the right to rectification?
0|What is the right to rectification?.answer:
- The data subject can demand that the controller correct inaccurate personal data without undue delay. [Art. 16, p. 43]
- The data subject can request that incomplete personal data be completed, possibly by providing a supplementary statement. [Art. 16, p. 43]

Sources:
- Art. 16, p. 43: "The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller without undue delay the rectification of inaccurate personal data concerning him or her. | Taking into account the purposes of the processing, the data subject shall have the right to have incomplete personal data completed, including by means of providing a supplementary statement."

0|What is the right to restriction of pr.q: What is the right to restriction of processing?
0|What is the right to restriction of pr.answer:
- Restriction of processing means marking stored personal data so that its future processing is limited. [Art. 4(3), p. 33]
- A data subject may request the controller to restrict processing when one of the specified situations applies. [Art. 18, p. 44-45]

Sources:
- Art. 4(3), p. 33: "(3) ‘restriction of processing’ means the marking of stored personal data with the aim of limiting their processing in the future;"
- Art. 18, p. 44-45: "The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller restriction of processing where one of the following applies:"

0|What is the right to object to process.q: What is the right to object to processing?
0|What is the right to object to process.answer:
- A data subject may object at any time to processing based on Article 6(e) or (f), including profiling, on grounds related to their particular situation, and the controller must stop unless it can show compelling legitimate grounds. [Art. 21(1), p. 45]
- For direct marketing, the data subject can object at any time to the processing of their personal data, which also covers profiling linked to that marketing. [Art. 21(2), p. 45]
- If the data subject objects to direct marketing, the controller must cease processing the personal data for those purposes. [Art. 21(3), p. 45]
- The right to object must be explicitly communicated to the data subject by the latest time of the first communication and presented clearly and separately from other information. [Art. 21(4), p. 46]
- When using information society services, the data subject may exercise the right to object through automated means using technical specifications. [Art. 21(5), p. 46]
- For scientific, historical or statistical research, the data subject can object on personal grounds unless the processing is necessary for a task carried out for reasons of public interest. [Art. 21(6), p. 46]

Sources:
- Art. 21(1), p. 45: "1. The data subject shall have the right to object, on grounds relating to his or her particular situation, at any time to processing of personal data concerning him or her which is based on point (e) or (f) of Article 6(1), including profiling based on those provisions."
- Art. 21(2), p. 45: "Where personal data are processed for direct marketing purposes, the data subject shall have the right to object at any time to processing of personal data concerning him or her for such marketing, which includes profiling to the extent that it is related to such direct marketing."
- Art. 21(3), p. 45: "Where the data subject objects to processing for direct marketing purposes, the personal data shall no longer be processed for such purposes."
- Art. 21(4), p. 46: "At the latest at the time of the first communication with the data subject, the right referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 shall be explicitly brought to the attention of the data subject and shall be presented clearly and separately from any other information."
- Art. 21(5), p. 46: "In the context of the use of information society services, and notwithstanding Directive 2002/58/EC, the data subject may exercise his or her right to object by automated means using technical specifications."
- Art. 21(6), p. 46: "Where personal data are processed for scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes pursuant to Article 89(1), the data subject, on grounds relating to his or her particular situation, shall have the right to object to processing of personal data concerning him or her, unless the processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out for reasons of public interest."

0|What rights apply to automated decisio.q: What rights apply to automated decision-making and profiling?
0|What rights apply to automated decisio.answer:
- Data subjects have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them. [Art. 22, p. 46]
- This right does not apply if the decision is necessary for entering into or performance of a contract between the data subject and a controller. [Art. 22, p. 46]
- When the decision falls under the contract or consent exceptions, the controller must provide at least the right to obtain human intervention, express the data subject’s point of view, and contest the decision. [Art. 22, p. 46]
- Data subjects have the right to be informed of the existence of automated decision‑making, including profiling, and to receive meaningful information about the logic, significance and envisaged consequences of such processing. [Art. 15(1), p. 43]
- Controllers must provide the information on automated decision‑making and profiling (including logic, significance and envisaged consequences) to the data subject at the time personal data are obtained. [Art. 13(2), p. 41]
- Suitable safeguards for automated decision‑making must include the right to obtain human intervention, to express a point of view, to obtain an explanation of the decision and to challenge it. [Recital 71, p. 14]

Sources:
- Art. 22, p. 46: "The data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her. | 1. Paragraph 1 shall not apply if the decision: (a) is necessary for entering into, or performance of, a contract between the data subject and a data controller; | In the cases referred to in points (a) and (c) of paragraph 2, the data controller shall implement suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests, at least the right to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, to express his or her point of view and to contest the decision."
- Art. 15(1), p. 43: "1. (h) the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, referred to in Article 22(1) and (4) and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject."
- Art. 13(2), p. 41: "(f) the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, referred to in Article 22(1) and (4) and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject."
- Recital 71, p. 14: "In any case, such processing should be subject to suitable safeguards, which should include specific information to the data subject and the right to obtain human intervention, to express his or her point of view, to obtain an explanation of the decision reached after such assessment and to challenge the decision."

0|When must a data protection officer be.q: When must a data protection officer be designated?
0|When must a data protection officer be.answer:
- The text states: "The controller and the processor shall designate a data protection officer in any case where" [Art. 37(1), p. 55]
- In all other situations, the controller or processor may designate a data protection officer, but must do so if Union or Member State law requires it. [Art. 37(4), p. 55]

Sources:
- Art. 37(1), p. 55: "The controller and the processor shall designate a data protection officer in any case where:"
- Art. 37(4), p. 55: "In cases other than those referred to in paragraph 1, the controller or processor or associations and other bodies representing categories of controllers or processors may or, where required by Union or Member State law shall, designate a data protection officer."

0|What are the tasks of the data protect.q: What are the tasks of the data protection officer?
0|What are the tasks of the data protect.answer:
- The DPO must inform and advise the controller, processor and their employees about their obligations under the Regulation and other Union or Member State data‑protection provisions. [Art. 39, p. 56]
- The DPO must monitor compliance with the Regulation, other Union or Member State data‑protection provisions and the controller’s or processor’s policies concerning the protection of personal data. [Art. 39, p. 56]
- The DPO must provide advice on data‑protection impact assessments when requested and monitor their performance. [Art. 39, p. 56]
- The DPO must cooperate with the supervisory authority. [Art. 39, p. 56]
- The DPO must act as the supervisory authority’s contact point on processing issues, including prior consultation and any other matters as appropriate. [Art. 39, p. 56]

Sources:
- Art. 39, p. 56: "(a) to inform and advise the controller or the processor and the employees who carry out processing of their obligations pursuant to this Regulation and to other Union or Member State data protection provisions; (b) to monitor compliance with this Regulation, with other Union or Member State data protection provisions and with the policies of the controller or processor in relation to the protection of personal data, including the assignment of responsibilities, awareness-raising and training… | (c) to provide advice where requested as regards the data protection impact assessment and monitor its performance pursuant to Article 35; | (d) to cooperate with the supervisory authority; (e) to act as the contact point for the supervisory authority on issues relating to processing, including the prior consultation referred to in Article 36, and to consult, where appropriate, with regard to any other matter."

0|When is a data protection impact asses.q: When is a data protection impact assessment required?
0|When is a data protection impact asses.answer:
- A DPIA is required when a type of processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. [Art. 35(1), p. 53]
- A DPIA is required for a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal effects or significantly affects the natural person. [Art. 35(3), p. 53]
- A DPIA is required for processing on a large scale of special categories of data or of personal data concerning criminal convictions and offences. [Art. 35(3), p. 53]
- A DPIA is required for systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale. [Art. 35(3), p. 53]

Sources:
- Art. 35(1), p. 53: "Where a type of processing in particular using new technologies, and taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall, prior to the processing, carry out an assessment of the impact of the envisaged processing operations on the protection of personal data."
- Art. 35(3), p. 53: "(a) a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects relating to natural persons which is based on automated processing, including profiling, and on which decisions are based that produce legal effects concerning the natural person or similarly significantly affect the natural person; | (b) processing on a large scale of special categories of data referred to in Article 9(1), or of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10; | or (c) a systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale."

0|When must the controller consult the s.q: When must the controller consult the supervisory authority before processing?
0|When must the controller consult the s.answer:
- The controller must consult the supervisory authority before processing when a data protection impact assessment shows the processing would pose a high risk without mitigation. [Art. 36(1), p. 54]
- Member State law can require the controller to consult and obtain prior authorisation from the supervisory authority for processing that implements a public‑interest task. [Art. 36(5), p. 55]

Sources:
- Art. 36(1), p. 54: "The controller shall consult the supervisory authority prior to processing where a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 indicates that the processing would result in a high risk in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate the risk."
- Art. 36(5), p. 55: "Notwithstanding paragraph 1, Member State law may require controllers to consult with, and obtain prior author­ isation from, the supervisory authority in relation to processing by a controller for the performance of a task carried out by the controller in the public interest, including processing in relation to social protection and public health."

0|When must the controller inform data s.q: When must the controller inform data subjects about a personal data breach?
0|When must the controller inform data s.answer:
- The controller must inform data subjects without undue delay when the breach is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms. [Art. 34(1), p. 52]
- The controller does not have to inform data subjects if it has taken subsequent measures that ensure the high risk is no longer likely to materialise. [Art. 34(3), p. 53]

Sources:
- Art. 34(1), p. 52: "When the personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall communicate the personal data breach to the data subject without undue delay."
- Art. 34(3), p. 53: "(b) the controller has taken subsequent measures which ensure that the high risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects referred to in paragraph 1 is no longer likely to materialise;"

0|What information must be given when pe.q: What information must be given when personal data is collected from the data subject?
0|What information must be given when pe.answer:
- The controller must give the data subject the identity and contact details of the controller and, where applicable, its representative. [Art. 13(1), p. 40-41]
- The controller must give the data subject the contact details of the data protection officer, where applicable. [Art. 13(1), p. 40-41]
- The controller must give the data subject the purposes of the processing and the legal basis for the processing. [Art. 13(1), p. 40-41]
- If processing is based on point (f) of Article 6(1), the controller must disclose the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or a third party. [Art. 13(1), p. 40-41]
- The controller must give the data subject the recipients or categories of recipients of the personal data, if any. [Art. 13(1), p. 40-41]
- Where applicable, the controller must inform the data subject that it intends to transfer personal data to a third country or international organisation and whether an adequacy decision exists. [Art. 13(1), p. 40-41]
- The controller must tell the data subject the period for which the personal data will be stored, or the criteria used to determine that period if the period cannot be specified. [Art. 13(2), p. 41]
- The controller must inform the data subject of the right to request access, rectification, erasure, or restriction of processing of their personal data. [Art. 13(2), p. 41]
- If processing is based on consent, the controller must inform the data subject of the right to withdraw consent at any time without affecting prior lawful processing. [Art. 13(2), p. 41]
- The controller must inform the data subject of the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority. [Art. 13(2), p. 41]
- The controller must tell the data subject whether providing personal data is a statutory or contractual requirement and the consequences of not providing it. [Art. 13(2), p. 41]
- The controller must inform the data subject of any automated decision‑making, including profiling, and provide meaningful information about the logic involved. [Art. 13(2), p. 41]
- Paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 do not apply where the data subject already has the information. [Art. 13(4), p. 41]

Sources:
- Art. 13(1), p. 40-41: "(a) the identity and the contact details of the controller and, where applicable, of the controller's representative; | (a) the identity and the contact details of the controller and, where applicable, of the controller's representative; (b) the contact details of the data protection officer, where applicable; | (c) the purposes of the processing for which the personal data are intended as well as the legal basis for the processing; | 1. (d) where the processing is based on point (f) of Article 6(1), the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or by a third party; | (e) the recipients or categories of recipients of the personal data, if any; | (f) where applicable, the fact that the controller intends to transfer personal data to a third country or international organisation and the existence or absence of an adequacy decision by the Commission, or in the case of transfers referred to in Article 46 or 47, or the second subparagraph of Article 49(1), reference to the appropriate or suitable safeguards and the means by which to obtain a copy of them or where they have been made available."
- Art. 13(2), p. 41: "(a) the period for which the personal data will be stored, or if that is not possible, the criteria used to determine that period; | (b) the existence of the right to request from the controller access to and rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing concerning the data subject or to object to processing as well as the right to data portability; | (c) where the processing is based on point (a) of Article 6(1) or point (a) of Article 9(2), the existence of the right to withdraw consent at any time, without affecting the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal; | (d) the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority; | (e) whether the provision of personal data is a statutory or contractual requirement, or a requirement necessary to enter into a contract, as well as whether the data subject is obliged to provide the personal data and of the possible consequences of failure to provide such data; | (f) the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, referred to in Article 22(1) and (4) and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject."
- Art. 13(4), p. 41: "Paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 shall not apply where and insofar as the data subject already has the information."
